planting.note: Start seed indoors with a cold-moist pretreatment or scarification, then transplant after frost danger has passed; established plants tolerate dry, poor, rocky soils far better than wet or fertile ones.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil and avoid rich or regularly irrigated beds, which shorten this Mediterranean shrub's life. Harvest the aromatic, downy young leaves and flowering tips in late spring to early summer and air-dry them for a tannin-rich, lemony herbal infusion popular across southern Europe. Plants resent root disturbance, so site them where they can remain undisturbed for years. Prune lightly after the pink, crepe-paper flowers fade to keep growth compact and encourage fresh leaf production.

common_name: Pindos Mountain Tea (Shepherd's Tea, Olympus Tea)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a gritty mix and transplant after frost into very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil; established clumps are drought-tolerant alpine natives.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, gravelly or rocky soil in full sun, mimicking the limestone cliffs of the Greek mountains it comes from. Cut the silvery-woolly flowering stems with their pale yellow blooms in mid to late summer and hang them to dry for a honey-sweet, slightly resinous infusion traditionally drunk for colds and as a daily tonic. Avoid heavy or moisture-retentive soils, which quickly rot the woody base. Divide congested clumps or take basal cuttings in spring to maintain vigor, since plants can decline after several years in overly rich ground.

planting.note: Start indoors well before the last frost and transplant only once nights stay reliably warm; in frost-prone climates grow as a container plant brought inside for winter.

directions: Grow this Southern African shrub in full sun with moderate, well-drained soil and protection from frost, which kills it outright. Pick the lemon-and-camphor-scented leaves fresh or dried year-round for a traditional bush tea widely used across Southern Africa to ease coughs, colds, and fevers. The small white flower clusters attract pollinators through the warm season. Cut plants back hard in early spring to renew growth and keep the naturally sprawling habit tidy.

planting.note: Pretreat hard seed coats with hot water or scarification before sowing; transplant into acidic, sandy, low-phosphorus soil similar to its native fynbos habitat.

directions: Plant in acidic, sandy, fast-draining soil that mimics the fynbos mountain slopes of South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape, and avoid phosphorus-rich fertilizers, which this legume shrub cannot tolerate. The commercially most important honeybush species, its needle-like leaves and stems are cut, bruised, and fermented in the sun to develop the characteristic sweet, honey-like flavor used for caffeine-free tea. It needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and cannot handle prolonged humidity or waterlogged roots. Established plants are fire-adapted and resprout or reseed readily after periodic burning or hard cutback.

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-treat seed before sowing; transplant into lean, sandy, coastal-type soil and avoid rich garden beds.

directions: Grow in lean, sandy, well-drained soil near the coast, where this low-lying South African shrub naturally thrives among coastal fynbos. Its yellow pea-like flowers give way to needle-fine leaves that are cut, bruised, and sweated to produce the original honeybush tea of the Western Cape, prized for a milder, more floral character than Cyclopia intermedia. Plants dislike humid, waterlogged conditions and perform best with dry summers and winter rainfall patterns. Prune after flowering to maintain a dense habit and stimulate fresh leafy growth for harvest.

common_name: Rico Red Roselle (Rico Red Hibiscus Tea)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm soil and transplant only after all frost danger has passed and nights stay warm; a long, hot growing season is needed to ripen the calyces before fall frost.

directions: Grow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture through summer to push this fast-growing roselle selection to a heavy calyx set before shortening days trigger flowering. Harvest the plump, deep-red calyces soon after the flowers drop and before seed pods toughen, then dry or simmer them fresh for a tart, cranberry-colored infusion. As a short-day bloomer, flowering and calyx production are delayed until day length shortens in late summer, so give it the longest frost-free window possible. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, which multiplies the number of calyx-bearing side shoots at harvest.
